title: The “weird and complicated” world of oracy
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau answers Tom Sherrington's complaint that critics find oracy weird and complicated by listing contradictory claims made about it, then setting out five reasons oracy might be great and five reasons for caution, applying a principle of charity. On the positive side he accepts that talk opens doors, that some children get far more practice than others, that talk is a cognitive lever, that formal speaking must be taught, and that insisting on full answers stops children hiding. The cautions are that speaking and listening assessment was tried and abandoned at GCSE, that nobody agrees what oracy is, that it is hard to assess by sampling, that the evidence is disappointing, and that nobody can talk well about what they do not know. He proposes vivas that judge content over delivery as a fairer approach. The common ground is that pupils should talk purposefully and answer in full, but Didau parts company with treating talk as a separable skill with equal status to reading and writing.
points: Oracy means whatever the speaker wants it to mean, so productive argument needs a definition before it needs a position.
Explicit teaching of rhetoric and structured access to formal speaking would give disadvantaged pupils the practice that middle-class children get at home.
Talk is a cognitive lever only when pupils know something to talk about and the teacher mediates the exchange.
Past GCSE speaking and listening marks were unreliable and inflated, and vague oracy descriptors invite teaching to the criteria and rewarding confidence over knowledge.
A viva that probes what a child knows, recorded and judged by more than one person, is a better way to assess talk than grading delivery.
quotes: You don’t have to think all of these are daft to accept that an idea which can hold all of them at once is at least a bit weird and complicated.

Everything that matters in adult life gets decided, at some point, by talking. Those who can explain themselves clearly and argue their case under pressure get listened to, and those who can’t are talked over.
Middle-class children pick up the codes of power at home and round the dinner table whatever any framework says. The children who most need to break these codes will only learn to do so in school.
When we ask children to explain and justify what they think, we aren’t giving them a break from thinking, we’re giving them the tools to do it.

Nobody wants to make school a misery for them but letting them off is not a kindness. Avoiding the things we’re afraid of usually makes them loom larger, and the children most likely to opt out are often the ones with most to gain from taking part.

When children who know something talk about it, they can sharpen, test and extend what they know. When they don’t, they pool their ignorance. Confident wrong answers spread round a group far faster than a hesitantly expressed correct answer.

Faced with vague criteria, we fall back on what we can see and hear. Eye contact, volume, pace and a confident manner are easy to spot. Whether students understand what they’re talking about is much harder.

Where I part company with the oracy movement is over whether talk can be taught, assessed and given “equal status” as if it were a separate thing. What children are able to say depends on what they know.
context: Contradictory claims about oracy show how loosely the term is used.
Success in adult life depends on speaking, so children who cannot speak are disadvantaged.
Only school can teach the codes of power to children who do not absorb them at home.
Making children explain what they think strengthens their reasoning.
Excusing anxious pupils from speaking lowers expectations and entrenches their avoidance.
Unstructured group talk can spread misconceptions instead of correcting them.
Vague oracy rubrics reward visible confidence rather than understanding.
What pupils can say is limited by what they know, so oracy cannot stand alone.
